title: Finegold Once Said "Never Play F5" | Latvian Gambit | A GM Naroditsky Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: This game illustrates how bad f5 is across most openings — it opens the king's diagonal and permanently weakens the kingside. The Dutch is the one exception, and only because White hasn't touched the e-pawn, so that diagonal stays closed; even so, against d4 it's dubious and the Staunton Gambit is no joke.
moves.teaches: f5 is only sound when the e-file diagonal to your king is still closed; otherwise it's a lasting weakness.

moves.spoken: So we answer with e4, the Staunton Gambit — a pawn for a big lead in development and open lines against the loosened king.
Nxe5 snaps the pawn, and this is the recurring nightmare of an early f-pawn push: the king is bare to Qh5-check ideas, and a knight sacrifice on e5 opens the floodgates.
moves.teaches: An early ...f5/...f6 invites Nxe5 and Qh5+ — the same king-hunt that refutes the Damiano.

moves.spoken: Bc4 looks like it's biting on nothing, but it threatens Nf7 — and Black is so far behind in development that almost any sacrifice lands.
moves.teaches: Against an undeveloped king, aim at f7 and trust that the sacrifices will work.

moves.spoken: Nxd5 sacrifices a knight to blow open the h5-e8 line for a check on h5 — with the king this exposed, material is a secondary concern.
moves.teaches: Sacrifice to open the checking line at a stuck king; the initiative outweighs the piece.

moves.spoken: Now the motifs cascade: with a knight near the king, g6 fails to the capture; take the pawn rather than the rook to keep the attack; and Be6-check sets up a winning discovery or skewer. The king gets driven to the queenside and hunted down.
moves.teaches: In a king-hunt, prefer the move that keeps the attack flowing over the one that grabs material.

moves.spoken: When the smoke clears we simply recapture cleanly and stand a piece up with a raging position — the whole line is one long lesson in developing before you push pawns.
moves.teaches: Develop your pieces before pushing wing pawns; the f-pawn lunge is where disasters begin.

moves.spoken: One caveat: f5 isn't always losing. The Schliemann in the Ruy isn't refuted — White is just better — because there the Spanish bishop isn't ideally placed to punish it. These verdicts are concrete to the position, never universal laws.
moves.teaches: Opening judgments are position-specific; the same pawn push can be bad in one setup and playable in another.
